1:
The chapter opens on a pause in the march. puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the scene: Israel's tents were pitched in the plains of Moab, where they stayed many months, looking back on the conquest of Sihon and Og and forward to Canaan. In that pause the disposal of what they had already taken was concerted and settled — not by any particular order or appointment of God, Henry stresses, but at the special instance and request of two of the tribes, to which Moses consented after a long debate. Even in an age of open miracle, he observes, many things were left to the direction of human prudence, for God in governing both the world and the church makes use of the reason of men.

The occasion is livestock. reformed John Gill observes that these two tribes evidently had more cattle in proportion than any of the others, though by what means is not easy to say; very probably they were more addicted to the pastoral life, took more delight in breeding, and were more diligent in the care of their herds. Henry weighs the same fact differently. It was supposed they had brought more out of Egypt, but that was forty years back, and stocks of cattle increase and decrease in less time than that; he thinks rather that these tribes had been better husbands of their beasts in the wilderness, not so profuse as their neighbours in eating the lambs out of the flock. reformed John Calvin traces the difference further back, to the district they had inhabited in Egypt, which being better suited for pasture had invited them to apply themselves more earnestly to a mode of life common to all the fathers.

For the country itself the grammatical-historical witnesses supply the map. Keil and Delitzsch note that the petitioners named "the land of Jazer, and the land of Gilead," putting Jazer first probably because that district was especially rich in excellent pasture land (Numbers 21:32), and that Gilead lay both south and north of the Jabbok — the modern Belka between the Jabbok and the Arnon, and Jebel Ajlun northward as far as the Mandhur — a country still showing numerous traces of great fertility. They mark the Hebrew too: me'od atsum, "very strong," stands as an apposition at the close of the sentence to give emphasis to the multitude. Charles Ellicott adds a reason of neighbourhood: Reuben and Gad had occupied contiguous positions in the encampment for thirty-eight years (Numbers 2:10, Numbers 2:14), and it was natural that they should wish to be permanently located near each other. wesleyan-arminian John Wesley identifies Jazer as a city and country of the Amorites, and Gilead as a mountainous country famous for pasturage.

What the seeing amounted to is where the reading turns severe. Calvin takes the verse as a glass in which we behold self-interest at work: they see a tract of rich and fertile land, and it does not occur to them that they lay under an obligation to their brethren not to covet anything peculiar or separate. He allows the pretext was specious — nothing was taken from the rest but rather added, and the army would advance in lighter condition without the herdsmen encumbering it — yet their association for the war bound them by an indissoluble tie. Henry cites that judgement approvingly and names the two springs of the choice as the lust of the eye and the pride of life (1 John 2:16): the land was not only pleasant to look at but good for food, food for cattle. Both draw the same warning from the single word saw: Lot chose by the sight of the eye and smarted for his choice, and would we choose our portion aright we must look above the things that are seen.
2:
A small change in the order of the names carries most of the comment here. Gill points out that the children of Gad are mentioned first though Reuben was the firstborn and Gad pitched under Reuben's standard; on the authority of Aben Ezra he thinks the Gadites were the authors of this counsel, the contrivers of the scheme, who first moved it to the Reubenites they lay encamped beside — or at the least that they were the most busy and active in the affair, or the best spokesmen. Henry notices the same inversion and reads it the same way: Reuben stands first in the opening verse, but Gad first afterwards, either because the Gadites made the first motion and were most forward for it, or because they had more of the art of management, Reuben's tribe still lying under Jacob's sentence that he should not excel. Gill adds the practical qualification that it could only have been some, in the name of the whole, who addressed Moses.

Who was addressed matters as much as who spoke. The petition went to Moses, to Eleazar the priest, and to the princes of the congregation together, and Calvin makes their modesty a point of praise: they neither detached themselves from the people nor seditiously and violently seized the places that suited them, but sought to obtain them by permission, as men submitting their cause to a decision not their own. Their request, he grants, was apparently a reasonable one — God had driven out the inhabitants, the fertility of the land invited them, and it seemed hard that empty and deserted fields should be denied. But private interest had so laid hold of their minds that the main point did not occur to them: the land of Canaan was set before them all, that they might dwell there together, separate from the heathen nations; and it was unjust that they should not only enjoy repose while the others fought, but be settled in an assured and peaceable habitation while ten tribes were still advancing to the conquest.

Keil and Delitzsch, reading the petition as a legal document rather than a moral one, note that the speakers go on to define the country more distinctly by naming a number of important towns, and that the clause describing it as the land the LORD smote before the congregation marks it as territory now without a ruler, and therefore easily taken possession of. On the closing words they are deliberately mild. "Let us not go over the Jordan" may be understood as expressing nothing more than the wish of the speakers not to receive their inheritance on the western side, without any intention of withdrawing their help from the other tribes in the conquest of Canaan — which is what their own later declaration claims. That charitable construction is not the one Moses put on it, and the difference between the two is what drives the rest of the chapter.
3:
A list of nine towns stands in for the whole request, and the witnesses treat it as a survey rather than a speech. Gill identifies the places as Amorite, taken from Sihon their king: of Ataroth, he says, we read nowhere else but in this chapter; Dibon he has already handled; Jazer was a city from which the surrounding land took its name, the same as Jaazer, and stood about fifteen miles from Heshbon, the capital city of Sihon's kingdom. wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke widens the frame: the places named here belonged to Sihon king of the Amorites and to Og king of Bashan, and being conquered by the Israelites they constituted ever after a part of their territories, as the grant later in the chapter makes formal.

Keil and Delitzsch treat the roll of names as the petitioners' way of fixing the boundaries of what they were asking for, and defer the geography itself to the closing section, where the same towns are listed again as the tribes rebuild them. The effect of that deferral is worth noticing. At this point in the narrative the names function as a claim; by the end of the chapter they will function as an inventory of what was actually settled and fortified, and several of the towns will have changed hands between Gad and Reuben in the process.
4:
Before they name their wish the petitioners name its title. Gill observes that the country in which those cities stood — with perhaps others not mentioned — was now in the hands of the people of Israel, and that the conquest of it is ascribed to the LORD, for the victory was his: it was he who smote their enemies and delivered the country into their hands. The petitioners say as much themselves in the very clause by which they identify the ground they are asking for, so that the title they plead is one they have just acknowledged is not their own making. From that Gill draws the constitutional point behind the request. Because the land had come to the nation as a whole, Moses, Eleazar and the princes of the congregation, being the representatives of the people, had a right to dispose of it; which is precisely what these two tribes were asking them to do, and the reason they gave for asking follows immediately.

Keil and Delitzsch read the same clause as a legal description of the property. To call it the country which the LORD smote before the congregation is to describe a land that no longer has a ruler, and which could therefore be taken possession of without dispossessing anyone — a point that made the petition look, on its face, modest rather than grasping. They note the construction of the verb of giving with its object as one they have discussed at Genesis 4:18.

The argument as the speakers frame it is a syllogism of two premises, and both are true. The land is a land for cattle; thy servants have cattle. Henry, summarising the motion, allows that it was not unreasonable on its own terms: what they possessed by right of conquest belonged to Israel in common, and on the general idea they had of the land of promise they supposed this tract would be about their due proportion. The trouble is not in either premise but in what the speakers leave out of the conclusion — that the promise ran to a land on the other side of the river, and that the fitness of a country for flocks is not the measure by which an inheritance from God is to be chosen. Every witness who takes the request apart does so at that joint.
5:
The request itself is put with great courtesy. Gill notes that the speakers direct their words to Moses as the ruler of the congregation, and in a modest, decent and respectable manner; Clarke gives the plain motive, that they asked for the land because it was good for pasturage and they had many flocks. Everything turns on the last clause, and Ellicott sets out the two ways it can be taken. "Bring us not over Jordan" may be understood simply as a request that the inheritance of the speakers be assigned on the eastern side of the river; or it may be understood, as Moses appears to have understood it and as Ellicott thinks it was in all probability designed to be understood, as a request that the conquest of the western side be left to the other tribes, and that Reuben and Gad be permitted to establish themselves at once in the country already subjugated. Ellicott allows a motive that is not simply cowardice: judging by the ease and rapidity with which the east had fallen, they may have thought their brethren well able to subdue the west without them.

Keil and Delitzsch prefer the milder reading, taking the words to express nothing more than a wish about where the inheritance should lie. Ellicott, whichever construction is adopted, holds the language indefensible in its effect — it indicated a selfish consideration of their own interests, and it was calculated to discourage and dishearten their brethren, and was therefore strongly reproved. He closes with an observation the reader is meant to feel: it is deserving of notice that Reuben, Gad and the half tribe of Manasseh were among the first who were carried into captivity by the king of Assyria (1 Chronicles 5:26).

Henry is blunter still, and careful to say why. At first sight the thing looked ill, and especially these closing words. It seemed to proceed from a contempt of the land of promise, which Moses himself so longed for a sight of, and from a distrust of the power of God to dispossess the Canaanites, as if a lot in a land already conquered were more desirable than a lot in a land yet to be won — one bird in the hand being reckoned worth two in the bush. It seemed covetous, since what they insisted on was that the country was convenient for their cattle. And it seemed a neglect of their brethren, as though they cared not what became of Israel so long as they themselves were well provided for. Henry adds a second order of danger: the people might have taken improper hints from it, reckoning themselves few enough with their whole number to face the Canaanites, and unequal indeed if two tribes and a half — above a fifth part of their strength — were dropped on this side of the river; and it would have set a precedent by which the regular disposal of the land by lot could have been anticipated tribe by tribe.
6:
Moses answers with a question, and the sharpness of it is itself a matter of comment. Gill records simply that he was displeased with the motion, as the following discourse shows, it having at first sight an appearance of covetousness and cowardice. Wesley catches the contrast the question is built on: ye sit here — in ease and peace, while your brethren are engaged in a bloody war.

Calvin refuses to let the vehemence be explained away. So sharp and severe a reproof shows us the greatness of the wrong; neither did inconsiderate warmth carry Moses into violent anger, nor did he fall into error and deliver an opinion on a point he did not understand. He knew what the sons of Gad and Reuben were asking, and inveighed against them thus vehemently because they desired to lacerate the body of the Church by this wicked severance. Calvin then separates two counts in the charge. The first is against their brethren: they sought to indulge in idleness while the rest marched through a hostile land, though they possessed no rightful superiority that would let them throw all the labours, perils and burdens of the war upon others; God had imposed the same condition upon all and had united them together, that they should keep company with each other. The second count is heavier, and Calvin says so expressly — their ingratitude and perverseness toward God is chastised more severely than their injustice toward their brethren, since the effect of the proposal would be that the hearts of the children of Israel should be broken, so that they would refuse to obey the call of God.

Henry, reading the same speech, insists that the heat is not temper. It is to be imputed to Moses' pious zeal against sin, and not to any peevishness as the effect of old age, for his meekness abated no more than his natural force. What Henry hears in the question is a holy indignation at selfishness: shall your brethren go to war and expose themselves to all the hardships and hazards of the field, and shall you sit here at your ease? The application he draws runs past the two tribes: it ill becomes any of God's Israel to sit down unconcerned in the difficult and perilous concernments of their brethren, whether public or personal. Henry also thinks the rebuke worked, and says so later in the chapter — it was by showing them their sin and its danger that Moses brought them to their duty without murmuring or disputing.
7:
The second question names the injury. Gill spells out the arithmetic of it: if these tribes settled on this side Jordan, Israel would lose the assistance of two tribes, two thirds of one of their standards, in fighting their enemies and subduing the land. But he thinks the discouragement would be moral before it was military. The request might be thought to proceed from selfish views and a love of ease, which would set a bad example to others; and it carried in it a distrust of ever being able to enter, much less to conquer and possess, the land of Canaan — and a distrust of that kind spreads.

Ellicott works on the verb. The word rendered discourage means rather to alienate or to avert, and its cognate noun occurs again two verses later in exactly the same connection, where the spies are said to have done the very same thing to the same people. Keil and Delitzsch put the charge in its sequence: by their disinclination the petitioners would take away the courage and inclination of the other tribes to cross the Jordan and conquer the land, and would bring the wrath of God upon Israel even more than their fathers did — the fathers who were sent from Kadesh-barnea to spy out the land, and who led the heart of the people away into rebellion by their unfavourable account of the inhabitants of Canaan. The Hebrew idiom they give for it is literally to hold the heart away from something.

Henry adds the reckoning that a general would make. The people might have taken improper hints from the proposal and concluded that they were few enough with their whole number to deal with the Canaanites; how unequal would the match be if two tribes and a half were dropped on this side of the river. Calvin had located the same danger in the previous verse, that the hearts of the children of Israel would be broken so that they would refuse to obey the call of God. All three converge on the same point: the harm Moses fears is not that the army will be smaller but that it will be unwilling, and the men who ask to stay behind will have made it so without lifting a hand.
8:
Moses now turns to history, and the phrase thus did your fathers is the hinge. Gill is careful about who is meant: not particularly and only the fathers of the two tribes Moses is addressing, but theirs and the other tribes' also, who acted much such a part — they did not choose to go into the good land to possess it when they were bid to, but were for sending spies first, whose ill report discouraged the people from going in at all. The recital that follows is Moses telling that story as a witness to it.

Calvin makes the comparison do more work than an illustration. He reads it as an amplification of the crime by reference to their continued perverseness, on the principle that the imitation of ungodly parents is so far from excusing children that it rather doubles their guilt. He gathers two other places where the same argument is made: Stephen's charge against the Jews of his own day, that they always resist the Holy Ghost, and as their fathers did, so do they (Acts 7:51); and the psalm that exhorts a later generation to obedience by recalling the same forty years of provocation in the wilderness (Psalms 95:8-10). What Moses complains of, on this reading, is that there was no end or limit to their impiety, the sons inheriting their fathers' iniquity and not ceasing to resist God.

Calvin then adds a distinction that keeps the charge from being merely sweeping, and it is the sharpest thing in the section. Moses does not compare the Reubenites and Gadites to the whole people, but to the ten spies, from whom the sedition arose — because as far as in them lay, these men were turning the people aside from the right way. That is why the punishment is attached to the story: it was hardly to be expected that they would amend of their own accord, so Moses means at least to inspire them with terror, reminding them that when God dealt so severely with their fathers he gave a plain proof that their descendants would not go unpunished unless they were teachable and submissive. And the forty years were not a closed chapter. The vengeance God had threatened had been before their eyes to that very day, so that it behoved them to be as much affected by it as if they saw the hand of God still stretched out; whenever any man died in the desert, God set his seal again to his own sentence, lest it should be buried in oblivion. From that Calvin argues from the less to the greater: if God was so wroth with the multitude in general, how should the instigators themselves escape?
9:
Three verses carry the recital forward at speed, and Gill supplies what little the geography needs. The spies went up unto the valley of Eshcol — that is, he says, they went up the hill, for they were bidden to go up into the mountain, and proceeded on into the country until they came to the valley, or brook, of Eshcol, so called from the cluster of grapes they cut down there and carried back with them. The place that furnished the proof of the land's goodness is the place from which the discouragement came, and Moses puts the two together in one sentence without comment.

On the kindling of the anger Gill marks its double object: it burned against the spies who brought the ill report, and against all the people who were disheartened and murmured upon it — which, he adds pointedly, was above all things to be dreaded now, with the same choice standing before the same nation a second time. The oath that follows is quoted rather than expounded, since the sentence and its ground were given at length when it was first pronounced.

Calvin fastens on the reason attached to it. The expression is remarkable, he says — because they fulfilled not after me — whereby Moses signifies that there is nothing praiseworthy in the most vigorous course unless men persevere even to the goal. It is an exact reproach to men who have come thirty-eight years through the wilderness and now propose to stop one river short.
12:
The exception to the oath raises a small question of descent that the witnesses cannot quite settle. Gill states it plainly: whether Caleb or Jephunneh is the one called the Kenezite is not so easy to determine, though the latter rather seems the more correct. His reasons are cumulative. That Caleb should be called so from Kenaz the father of Othniel, who is said to be Caleb's brother, seems not agreeable, since it is not likely they were own brothers, or Caleb would not have given his daughter to him; and Jephunneh, not Kenaz, is always named as Caleb's father, unless that father had two names. Gill's own preference is that Jephunneh, and so Caleb after him, took the name from an ancestor called Kenaz. He reports Jarchi's different account, that Caleb was the son-in-law of Kenaz, and that Caleb's mother bore Othniel to him.

Clarke cuts the knot the same way and more briefly: it was Jephunneh who was the Kenezite, not Caleb, and Kenaz was probably the father of Jephunneh. Wesley takes the name back a generation further still, calling Kenaz his grandfather. Ellicott leaves the genealogy alone and points instead to the commendation, which is quoted here word for word from the sentence pronounced at Numbers 14:24 — that they have wholly followed the LORD. The two men named are the living proof of the clause Calvin drew out of the preceding verses: what was lacking in the rest was not a beginning but an end.
13:
The sentence is stated in its executed form. Gill notes only that the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel for murmuring against the report of the spies, and lets the forty years speak. Ellicott makes the connection explicit: Moses here declares the fulfilment of the prediction which he had himself announced, in obedience to the divine commandment, at the time when the spies brought up their evil report of the land (Numbers 14:33-34).

That is the force of the recital for the men standing in front of him. Moses is not telling a story he heard; he is the man who delivered the sentence and then watched it run its whole length, until all the generation that had done evil in the sight of the LORD was consumed. The wandering was neither an accident of the route nor a delay: it was the precise term God had named, and it ended only when the last of that generation was gone. Whatever the Reubenites and Gadites thought they were asking for, Moses has just shown them what a refusal to cross a border cost the last men who made one.
14:
The application arrives with a behold, and Gill hears in it more than a change of generations. To be risen up in their fathers' stead is to have succeeded them in their families, of which these men were now the heads, and in their substance, their flocks and their herds — and, Gill suggests, in their manners and evil dispositions as well. The inheritance Moses grants them is the one they did not ask for.

Calvin works on the noun. He takes the phrase to mean that by their evil doings they were filling up the measure of their fathers, as Jesus spoke of the Jews of his own time, and he reads the word rendered an increase as a climax. Those who translate it education, or offspring, or foster-children give a poor rendering; among the Hebrews the noun comes from the verb to increase and multiply, is literally an increase or a multiplication, and is on that account applied to usury. Here, Calvin argues, the sense the passage requires is a heap: a new body of persons springing up afresh who carry impiety to its very height. His image for the effect is exact — fuel added to a fire that was smouldering, whereby a new flame is excited. They were furnishing materials for God's wrath, so that it should burst forth more and more against the whole people.

Henry sets the same verse against Moses' own hopes and finds the reversal painful. It was an encouragement to him to see what an increase of men there had been in these two tribes; it was a discouragement to see that it was withal an increase of sinful men, treading in the steps of their fathers' impiety. We hoped, he has Moses say, that you had risen up in their stead to possess the pleasant land, and you have risen up in their stead to despise it. Henry generalises the grief without softening it: it is sad to see the rising generation, in families and in countries, not only no better but worse than the one that went before it — and what comes of it is that the anger of the LORD is not merely continued but augmented, until the measure fills and overflows.
15:
Moses states the consequence as a conditional, and the witnesses take the condition seriously. Gill glosses the turning away as a turning from following God in the way of his commandments, from attending upon his word, worship and ordinances, and from walking after him who went before them in the pillar of cloud and fire — which is what stopping short here, and not going over Jordan into the land of Canaan, would amount to. The image is worth holding: the pillar was still moving westward, and to settle east of the river was to let it go on without them.

Keil and Delitzsch render the Hebrew idiom literally — if ye draw back behind him — and define it as resisting the fulfilment of the will of God to bring Israel to Canaan. The two clauses of the threat they take in order: he will leave Israel still longer in the desert, and ye prepare destruction for all this nation. The grammar is what makes the sentence terrible. The subject of the sin is two tribes; the object of the punishment is the whole congregation, and the verb in the second clause makes the petitioners themselves the agents of that ruin rather than its bystanders. Moses has just finished recounting what the last such refusal cost — forty years, and every man of a generation but two — so the threat is not rhetorical enlargement. It is the same sentence, described as available a second time.

Henry presses precisely that. What Moses gives them is fair warning of the mischief likely to follow upon the separation they were proposing to make from the camp: they would be in danger of bringing wrath upon the whole congregation and hurrying them all back again into the wilderness. Out of it he draws the maxim the chapter is remembered for as much as any verse in it — if men did but consider, as they ought, what would be the end of sin, they would be afraid of the beginnings of it. Nothing has yet happened. Nobody has crossed anything, or refused to. The whole of what Moses is describing still lies inside a request made politely by men who have not yet done anything wrong, and that is the point of describing it.
16:
The answer begins with a movement. Gill notices that the heads of the two tribes came a little nearer to Moses, having something more to say to him, and used some degree of freedom and boldness in the saying of it. Henry reconstructs the interval: probably the petitioners withdrew, considered with themselves what answer they should return to so severe a reproof, and after some consultation came back with this proposal — that their men of war should go and assist their brethren in the conquest of Canaan, while their families and flocks stayed behind. Calvin reads the pause the same way, and draws from the reply a conclusion about the rebuke: from their answer we gather how usefully the severity of Moses had influenced their minds, for had he dealt with them more mildly his kindness would perhaps have been received with contempt. It was more profitable that their stubborn hearts should be smitten with shame and fear.

Whether the offer had been in their minds from the first, Henry frankly cannot tell, and he works out both possibilities. If it had, then here is an instance of how often what is honestly meant is unhappily misinterpreted — though Moses was excusable, having reason to suspect the worst, and his rebuke came from an abundance of care to prevent sin. If it had not, then here is an instance of the good effect of plain dealing, since by showing them their sin and its danger Moses brought them to their duty without murmuring or disputing. Calvin notes what they did not do: they do not altogether abandon their request, but devise a middle course, by which without forsaking their brethren they may still occupy the land — promising to accompany the whole expedition, and to be the first to undergo danger, provided a settled abode be granted for their families and herds.

On the two things they propose to build, the grammatical-historical witnesses are precise. Keil and Delitzsch describe the sheepfolds as pens built of stones piled one upon another (1 Samuel 24:4), and cite Wetstein's observation that nomads in the Leja still surround each camping place with an enclosure of stones about the height of a man, so that the flocks are not scattered in the night and the noise of the smaller stones laid along the top gives warning if a wolf attempts to climb in. By the building of towns, they add, we are to understand rebuilding and fortification. Ellicott agrees on both counts — the folds commonly constructed of loose stones piled up, and the verb build often meaning to build up or to repair, as it probably does here. Clarke argues the point from the impossibility of the alternative: numerous as these tribes were, they could not have built cities and fortified them for the defence of their families in their absence, and he follows Calmet in supposing they meant no more than repairing the Amorite cities they had lately taken, which could easily be accomplished in the months they still had east of the river.

Calvin closes the section with an accounting that is neither cynical nor naïve. On this arrangement they would be exempt from guilt, since the rest would not be held back by their bad example, nor the strength of the people for carrying on the war be diminished; in one respect only would they have the advantage — that by depositing their wives and children in a peaceful spot they would have the opportunity of improving their domestic affairs.
17:
What they offer is not merely to come, but to go first. Gill reads the emphasis as a direct answer to the charge: they said this to free themselves from the imputation of cowardice, and to show they did not mean to sit still while their brethren went to war; they were willing to put on their armour, meet the enemy on the borders of the land, and expose their own lives in favour of their brethren. Ellicott renders the phrase more exactly still — we will equip ourselves in haste — which turns a promise of presence into a promise of speed.

The second half of the verse raises a practical difficulty, and Clarke will not let it pass. If the little ones were to dwell in the fenced cities because of the inhabitants of the land — the Ammonites, Moabites, Idumeans, and the remains of the Midianites and Amorites — could women and children hold those cities by themselves? Certainly not, he answers, and therefore many of the men of war must have stayed behind. He then does the arithmetic. At the last census Reuben numbered 43,730 and Gad 40,500; Manasseh numbered 52,700, of which the half tribe is 26,350 — 110,580 men in all. From Joshua 4:13 we learn that only 40,000 of the two tribes and a half passed over Jordan to help their brethren. Consequently 70,580 remained for the defence of the women, the children and the flocks, which Clarke thinks more than sufficient against neighbours already panic-struck by their late defeats. Wesley reaches the same conclusion from the words themselves: we ourselves means either all, or as many as shall be thought necessary, leaving only so many as may be needed for the sustenance and defence of their families.

Ellicott adds a note on the term rendered little ones, which appears to include the whole defenceless portion of the nation rather than infants only (Exodus 12:37). Keil and Delitzsch keep the sense of the pledge in view: the men would go equipped before the children of Israel until they had brought them to their place — that is, until Israel was in Canaan. The undertaking is therefore open-ended in time and closed only by an event, and it is that shape, rather than any number of soldiers, that Moses takes up in his reply.
18:
Two further clauses complete the offer, and both give something away. Gill takes the first at its full weight: they will not return unto their houses — meaning the cities they were to build or repair, and their families, and their substance, their flocks and their herds, all of which they would leave behind and not so much as think of returning to until every man in Israel had his inheritance. The condition of their release is not a date, and not the fall of any particular city, but the settlement of the last of their brethren.

The second clause renounces a claim before anyone had thought to dispute it. Gill is careful about the spirit of it: they spoke so not as men who had determined the matter whether Moses and the princes were willing or not, and much less as despising the good land, but as giving up all pretensions to it if they were settled where they had asked to be. They were not, he says, of that selfish and covetous disposition which would have wanted a portion on the other side of Jordan as well as this one. Henry counts it as the fourth article of a fair and generous proposal, and hears them press the point positively — we will be content with our inheritance on this side, and there will be so much the more on yonder side for our brethren.

Ellicott finds a linguistic crux in the same sentence, and it is a genuinely interesting one. This is one of the critical passages that bear on the meaning of the term rendered on yonder side in the first clause and on this side in the second. He grants that the first is defined by the addition of the word rendered or forward — more correctly and forward, that is, further off — and that the second is defined by the addition of eastward, or towards the sunrising. But the application of one and the same word to the country on both banks shows that nothing can be inferred with any certainty from it about where the writer himself stood, as the same term recurs later in the chapter with no addition at all. Ellicott ends where Gill began: the language of the Gadites and Reubenites is not to be read as defiance, but as a disclaimer of any right to a portion west of the river if their request on the east were granted.
20:
Moses accepts, and the change of temper is the first thing Gill records: he was now better disposed toward them and more satisfied with the reasonableness of their request, it having been explained. But the terms Moses sets are not quite the terms they offered, and Henry puts his finger on the alteration. They had promised to go armed before the children of Israel; nay, says Moses, you shall go armed before the LORD. It is God's cause more than your brethren's, and to him you must have an eye, and not to them only.

Ellicott builds a good deal on that substitution, noting first that the verb and the preposition here are the same the speakers themselves had used, so that only the object has changed. From the expression it may be inferred that the army of Israel was regarded as the army of the LORD, and he thinks it probable that there is a reference to the ark being carried on certain occasions into the war. If the order of march laid down earlier was still observed, the tribes of Reuben and Gad, encamped on the south side of the tabernacle, immediately preceded the ark (Numbers 10:18-22), just as Ephraim, Benjamin and Manasseh immediately followed it (Psalms 80:2). At the passage of the Jordan the priests who bore the ark stood still in the river until the whole people had passed over before it (Joshua 4:5, 4:11); at the siege of Jericho the ark appears to have been carried in the midst of the host, some of the armed men going before and some following after (Joshua 6:9). If that is the true force of the phrase, Ellicott observes, it was natural that the spokesmen should first say before the children of Israel, and should not adopt before the LORD until Moses had used it of them first. Wesley reaches the same identification more directly: before the ark, which was the token of God's presence.

Calvin raises a difficulty that no one else in the chapter is willing to state so openly. Moses might seem to err on the side of excessive good-nature, in that he extends the boundaries prescribed by God to suit their wish: their inheritance had been promised in the land of Canaan, they ought to have been content with that, and it was not for Moses to make any alteration in a divine decree. There is a second oddity beside it — in a point of so much perplexity Moses does not, as usual, consult God, but gives an immediate answer. Calvin does not resolve this by excusing the request, which he calls by no means excusable, and which he says would never have entered their minds had they borne in memory the covenant of God. He resolves it from the outcome. God, who knows how to bring light out of darkness, not only pardoned their error but took occasion from it to extend his liberality, so that Bashan and its neighbourhood were added to the former boundaries; and the result vindicates Moses, since he commands that his ruling be ratified and maintained after his death, and the book of Joshua expressly excepts this country beyond Jordan from the allotment as having been granted by Moses. From that Calvin infers that the decision was approved by God, and he notes that Moses is repeatedly honoured there with the title of servant of God. Nor is it at random, he adds, that Moses makes such frequent use of the divine name in this very speech: he is implying throughout that what he does is suggested by God, and not by himself.
21:
Having granted the substance, Moses tightens every clause of the pledge. Gill sets out how thoroughly he tries them: he requires not merely that they go armed, or march from the place where they stood in the direction of Canaan, but that they go over Jordan; not some of them only, but all; and that before the LORD. Each addition closes a door through which the promise might later have been slipped. Henry hears the same insistence and states its practical form — Moses will have it that they should never lay down their arms till their brethren laid down theirs.

The end of the obligation is fixed by an event, and by an event that belongs to God rather than to the army. Until he hath driven out his enemies from before him: the enemies are his, the driving out is his, and the men who have just been told to march before the LORD are not to reckon their term finished by any success of their own. Every pronoun in that clause is God's, which is what allows Moses two verses later to hand them a possession held on the same terms — theirs, but before the LORD. It also settles a question the petitioners had left conveniently open. They had promised to serve until they had brought their brethren to their place, a term they could have judged fulfilled at almost any point after the first campaign; Moses replaces it with one only God can declare finished. Keil and Delitzsch, setting the sentence beside the ones that follow, treat verses twenty-one through twenty-four as a single conditional grant with its own penalty clause attached, which is why the language keeps returning to the same phrase.

Gill adds a note of fulfilment that reads oddly at first and then exactly. When the tribes actually came to the river, it was the ark, the symbol of the divine presence, that went first into Jordan and stood there while all the tribes passed over; and then these two tribes and the half tribe of Manasseh passed before the children of Israel and before the LORD unto battle. What Moses stipulates here as a condition is reported there as a fact, in almost the words he uses — which is as near as the narrative comes to telling the reader in advance that the pledge was kept.
22:
The grant is stated three times over in a single verse, and each time the same phrase is added. Gill takes the subduing first: the inhabitants fleeing before God's people and being conquered by them may well be said to be subdued before the LORD, since it was done in his presence, by his power, and for his people. Wesley glosses the phrase in its other bearing, as denoting God's presence with them and his gracious and powerful assistance.

Henry draws out what is granted on that condition, and it is more than land. They shall be guiltless before the LORD and before Israel; they shall have the possession, and neither sin nor blame shall cleave to it — neither sin before God nor blame before their brethren. His application is quietly searching: whatever possessions we have, it is desirable to come guiltless to them. The two courts named are not the same court, and the verse clears them in both. Ellicott points forward to where the settlement is recorded as accomplished fact, in the review of the eastern grant and in the allotment of Reuben and Gad under Joshua (Deuteronomy 3:12-20; Joshua 13:15-33).

What the verse does not say is as telling as what it does. It never calls the eastern country a second-best or a concession wrung out of Moses; it calls it their possession before the LORD, on the same footing and by the same authority as any lot west of the river. The condition is not on the title but on the men.
23:
The other half of the condition is now stated, and Moses states it as a certainty rather than a threat. Gill notes only that the failure in view is a failure to do as they had promised and as Moses insisted; the weight falls on what follows. Henry marks the direction of the offence: if you fail, you sin against the LORD, and not against your brethren only — God will certainly reckon with you for it, though you may make a light matter of it.

Calvin treats the words as a formal act. Moses makes a solemn protestation that they will deal wickedly if they break their promise, and denounces punishment against them as if he were summoning them before the tribunal of God. Though the engagement spoken of is a particular one, voluntarily undertaken by two tribes, Calvin derives the general doctrine without hesitation: unless we abide by our promises, God will always be the avenger of fraud and treachery. On the famous clause itself he is careful to say why the wording is stronger than a plainer one would have been. To say your sin will find you out is more emphatic than to say you shall not escape God's hand, for the meaning of it is that vengeance is so connected with sin that it cannot be severed from it. He sets beside it the sentence spoken to Cain, that sin lieth at the door (Genesis 4:7), waiting to lay hold at length upon the guilty. And he names the reason such a warning is needed at all: such is our propensity to sin that we are too often encouraged to audacity by God's forbearance, thinking we have escaped if for a time he makes as though he did not see us.

Wesley reads the pronoun as standing for its consequence — your sin, that is, the punishment of your sin — and turns the sentence into counsel. Sin will certainly find out the sinner sooner or later; it concerns us therefore to find our sins out, that we may repent of them and forsake them, lest they find us out to our confusion and destruction.

Then Moses closes by handing them back their own proposal as a command: build cities for your little ones and folds for your sheep. Gill notes the purpose plainly, the safety and security of the families and flocks, exactly as the petitioners had themselves proposed. The order of the two clauses in the command reverses theirs, putting the children before the cattle; and the last clause binds the whole — do that which hath proceeded out of your mouth. Nothing new is imposed. The obligation Moses lays on them is the one they invented for themselves, now spoken by the man who holds them to it.
25:
The answer is short, and Gill takes each clause as covering one half of the bargain: they will do as their lord commands, both with respect to their march before the LORD to battle and with respect to the provision they make for their children and their flocks. What follows is the inventory of what stays and what goes — the little ones, the wives, the flocks and all the cattle in the cities of Gilead; the men themselves over the river, every one armed for war.

Keil and Delitzsch notice that the promise is made once more, and that the verb which introduces it stands in the singular. Gill draws the same inference and reports Jarchi's way of putting it: the singular shows their unanimity, that they replied all of them as one man, and it may be that one spoke as the mouth of them all.

Henry treats the speech as a legal instrument. They agree unanimously to the provisos and conditions of the grant, and do as it were give bond for performance by a solemn promise. He also supplies the equity behind it, which the speakers do not state: their brethren had all contributed their assistance to the conquest of this eastern country which they were now asking for, and so they owned themselves obliged in justice to help in the conquest of what was to be their brethren's possession. Having received kindness, Henry adds, we ought to return it, even though it was not so conditioned when we received it.
28:
Moses does not leave the arrangement to rest on his own word, and the reason is given in the names he summons. Henry sees it at once: he settles this matter with Eleazar, and with Joshua who was to be his successor, knowing that he himself must not live to see it perfected. What he leaves behind is an estate upon condition — leaving it to Joshua, if the condition were fulfilled, to declare the estate absolute.

Gill reads the verse as a question of authority, and is careful not to overstate it. The wording looks as if Moses determined the case himself, though it was perhaps by the vote and with the consent of the whole court; what is certain is that Moses strictly enjoined the observance of it on those who would have to administer it. Calvin, coming to the same difficulty from the other side, insists that although Eleazar and the elders are not named as deciding anything, it is certain that they were not passed over but were united with Moses in the decision — the more so since the case had been brought before them jointly when the petition was first made.

On why the condition needed recording at all, Calvin is the most concrete. Moses annexes these terms to his decision so that, when the Reubenites and their companions had performed their military service, they could not afterwards be falsely alleged to have crossed the Jordan for the purpose of seeking a new home; and at the same time, should they deceive the other tribes, he provided that their cowardice and deceit should not profit them. The clause protects both parties, and it protects them against opposite accusations. A man who keeps his word will be able to point to the record when someone suggests he was only ever after a better portion; a man who breaks it will find the record waiting for him too.

The transfer of the whole business to Eleazar, Joshua and the chief fathers is also the first sign in the chapter that Moses is settling his affairs. He will not cross this river either. What he can do is fix the terms of a promise whose performance he will not see, and put them in the hands of the men who will.
29:
The instruction is given as a pair of alternatives, and both branches are spelled out so that no one has to interpret them later. Gill notes that Moses is speaking now to Eleazar, Joshua and the princes of the congregation rather than to the petitioners; the men who will execute the arrangement are told what to do in either event. If the two tribes pass over armed and the land is subdued, Gilead is to be given them for a possession. If they will not pass over armed, Gill glosses the case bluntly — should they change their minds, break their promise, and refuse to cross the river — then they shall have possessions among their brethren in the land of Canaan.

That second clause is easy to misread as an alternative gift, and the witnesses take pains over it. Wesley states the penalty in it: they shall forfeit their possessions in Gilead and be constrained to go over Jordan and to seek possessions there among their brethren. Henry hears the distinction in the very form of the sentence — Moses does not say you shall give them no inheritance at all, but you shall not give them this inheritance which they covet. If their fighting men will not come over, compel the whole tribes to come over; let them take their lot with their brethren and fare as they fare, and let them not expect that the lot will favour them.

Calvin reads the two branches as one settled principle. If they assist their brethren according to the agreement, the territory now granted is to remain theirs permanently; if they depart from their promise, they are to be forced against their will into the common allotment. He is explicit that this is not a consolation portion in the midst of Canaan awarded for inertness, but a compulsion — they should be forcibly and authoritatively carried onwards, and be subject to their brethren in every circumstance, since it was never lawful for them to consult their own separate interests. Calvin adds one further observation about the timing of the whole instruction. In laying down rules for the division of a land not yet entered, as though the division were soon to happen, Moses encourages the minds of all to confidence, so that they should the more cheerfully hasten to pass over — as if the victory were not only already in their hands, but its fruits about to be enjoyed.
31:
The reply is given by the two tribes together, and Gill draws attention to the form of the verb, which stands in the singular. It shows their unanimity, he says: they agreed to what Moses had said and answered all of them as one man, as Jarchi expresses it; and it may be that one served as the mouth of them all. Wesley opens out the appeal in their words. When they say as the LORD hath said unto thy servants, they may mean what God has said at this moment through the mouth of Moses, or they may reach back to what he commanded long before, when he charged them as well as their brethren to go into Canaan and possess it. On either reading they are no longer arguing from their cattle.

Then comes the sentence that closes the negotiation, and Gill notes that the substance of it has now been repeated again and again, for the confirmation of it, and to assure that it should be strictly performed according to its true intent. Keil and Delitzsch render the second half in the form the Hebrew gives it — we will pass over armed before Jehovah into the land of Canaan, and let our inheritance remain to us beyond the Jordan. The order of the two clauses is the whole of the concession: the crossing first and unconditional, the possession second and dependent on it. The term they use of their own inheritance here is the one Ellicott had picked out a dozen verses earlier as ambiguous, and he notes that it stands in this verse without any of the qualifying words that fixed its sense before — a reminder that the geography of the phrase is far less certain than the undertaking it is attached to.

One small thing has changed since the speakers first opened their mouths in this chapter. They asked at the beginning not to be brought over Jordan, and offered afterwards to go armed before the children of Israel; here they say they will go armed before the LORD, taking up the phrase Moses had pressed on them and making it their own. Henry marks the repetition simply as their adhering to their brethren; but the wording has travelled from a request about pasture to a promise made in the name of God, and the distance between the two is the distance the chapter has covered.
33:
The grant is made, and Gill wonders in what form. It may have been by word of mouth in the presence of the court, or, as he thinks more likely, by some instrument drawn up and signed by Moses and the elders, or at least witnessed by them. Calvin looks past the form to the authority behind it and is emphatic that Moses did not act on his own judgement: relying on God's command he laid down an inviolable law, and although it is nowhere expressly said that God interposed his authority here, the later approbation of the arrangement fully assures us of it. Calvin also hears an implied contrast running under the verse, between the old covenant God had made with Abraham and this new and special privilege with which he condescended to enrich his people.

What surprises every witness is the third name. Ellicott states the difficulty exactly: this is the first mention of the tribe of Manasseh, and the application for a grant east of the Jordan appears to have been made by Reuben and Gad alone. Keil and Delitzsch call it strange that the half-tribe should be included for the first time at the close of the negotiations, having gone entirely unmentioned in the negotiations themselves. The explanation both find is the one the next verses supply: a portion of Manasseh had been chiefly, if not exclusively, engaged in the conquest of certain parts of Gilead and Bashan, and had therefore justly acquired a claim to the districts it had subdued (Deuteronomy 3:13-15). Calvin says it in a sentence: half the tribe is now added, inasmuch as the descendants of Machir, Jair and Nobah, all of the family of Manasseh, had seized certain cities.

Henry offers a further reason and a piece of statecraft besides. Probably the half tribe had not joined in the petition at all; but the land, when it came to be apportioned, proved too much for two tribes, so this half tribe had a lot among them — perhaps at their own request, perhaps by divine direction, perhaps because they had distinguished themselves in the conquest of the country. The children of Machir were a stout and warlike family who had taken Gilead and dispossessed the Amorites, and Henry's verdict on that is cheerfully blunt: let them win it and wear it. Being celebrated for courage, they were also the right men to hold a frontier, and it was for the common safety to plant them there.

Keil and Delitzsch give the extent of the grant in the terms the Hebrew uses — the land according to its towns, with the districts belonging to them, the towns of the country round about — that is, the two kingdoms entire, of Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan, with everything that went with them. Nothing in this verse is conditional. The condition was recorded three verses back and lodged with Joshua; here the estate is simply conveyed, and the chapter turns from negotiation to settlement.
34:
The register of Gad's towns is not a building record, and the witnesses say so with one voice. Gill takes built to mean that they repaired the walls and fortifications and rebuilt the houses demolished in the wars with Sihon and Og, when those places were taken. Ellicott renders it repaired or fortified, and gives two reasons: some of the towns named — Dibon and Heshbon among them — appear already in the account of the Amorite conquest, so they plainly existed; and it is not probable that new cities would have been built at this moment, nor did the circumstances of Israel admit of the delay such an undertaking would have required. Wesley adds the practical form of the same point: the old cities had not been burnt and ruined, as several in Canaan afterwards were, so the settlers had neither need nor leisure as yet to do more than repair and fortify.

Keil and Delitzsch walk the list with a surveyor's care. Dibon, also called Dibon Gad, lay an hour's journey north of the central Arnon. Ataroth is probably preserved in the extensive ruins of Attarus on Jebel Attarus, between el Kureyat and Makur, the ancient Machaerus. Aroer they identify not as the Aroer before Rabbah, as v. Raumer supposed, but as the Aroer in the middle of the valley of the Arnon, still visible in the ruins of Araayr on the edge of the lofty rock wall that bounds the Modjeb. Atroth Shophan is named here and nowhere else, and its situation is unknown. Jaezer they place in the ruins of es Szir, west of Amman; Jogbehah, which occurs again only in the story of Gideon's pursuit (Judges 8:11), survives in the ruins of Jebeiha, some two hours north-west of Amman. Gill has less to add on this middle group, noting only that no mention is made of them elsewhere except Jaazer, which is the Jazer named at the head of the chapter; and on the last pair he supplies the afterlife of the names — Bethnimrah is the Nimrah of the earlier list, and Bethharan is the Betharam called Bethramtha in the Jerusalem Talmud and Bethramphta by the Syrians, the town to which Herod later gave the name of Livias, or Julias.

Two of the witnesses follow the towns down the centuries. Clarke takes Aroer on the Arnon as his example: it was formerly inhabited by the Emim, a warlike and perhaps gigantic people, who were expelled by the Moabites, the Moabites by the Amorites, and the Amorites by Israel; the Gadites then held it until their tribe went into captivity with Reuben and half Manasseh under the Assyrians (2 Kings 15:29), after which the Moabites appear to have repossessed it, since they seem to hold it in the oracle of Jeremiah (Jeremiah 48:15-20). Ellicott traces a shorter and stranger journey: in Joshua's distribution some of the southernmost towns repaired here by the Gadites fell to Reuben, while Heshbon, which the next verses credit to Reuben, fell to Gad and was afterwards assigned to the Levites. He also notes what one of these names has since yielded up — it was at Dibon that the Moabite stone was found in 1868.

The list closes on the two things the settlers had promised Moses they would make: fenced cities, and folds for sheep. The order in which the chapter has been reciting them is now reversed from the order in which they first asked, and the children are provided for before the flocks.
37:
Reuben's list is shorter and its towns better known. Gill identifies Heshbon as the royal city of Sihon king of the Amorites and Elealeh as lying within a mile of it, and takes the pair as proof that these places were not properly built anew but only repaired, since they had been standing cities long before. He adds the argument from the calendar: within a few months of this the tribes crossed the Jordan, which left no time for founding cities — though they left men enough behind, whom they might set to work when they departed. On the third name he collects what tradition offers: Kirjathaim is called by the Targum of Jonathan the city of two streets paved with marble, and identified there with Beresha; Jerome says it was known in his day as Coraiatha, ten miles from Medeba.

Keil and Delitzsch fix Heshbon on the ground and follow its title through the record. It stood almost midway between the Arnon and the Jabbok, opposite Jericho, twenty Roman miles from the river, where the ruins of a large town about a mile in circumference still bear the ancient name of Hesban, with deep bricked wells and a large reservoir among them. Allotted to Reuben, it was relinquished to Gad because it lay on the border of their territory, and given up by them in turn to the Levites. Elealeh they place half an hour north-east of Heshbon, now called el Aal, "the height," standing on a hilltop with a view over the whole southern country.

The last verse of the pair records something other than masonry, and here the witnesses divide over the motive. Gill takes it as an act of religion: Nebo was the name of an idol, after which the city was perhaps called, and Baalmeon signifies Baal's habitation, where it is highly probable a temple of his stood; the children of Reuben, not liking to retain such names, gave the towns others — though what they were is not recorded. Wesley allows two possible reasons, that conquerors of places were accustomed to rename them, or that the names of other gods, which Nebo and Baal-meon unquestionably were, were not to be mentioned at all (Exodus 23:13). Henry gives both with equal weight — either to show their authority, the change of names signifying the change of owners, or because the old names carried a respect to the deities worshipped there — and then throws his own weight behind the second, citing the same prohibition and the promise that God will take away the names of Baalim out of the mouths of his people (Hosea 2:17). Clarke reads the custom the other way about, and takes the renaming as the ordinary practice of conquerors, who called the cities they took after themselves — as Nobah did with Kenath at the close of the chapter.

Gill closes with a detail that gives the whole gesture a melancholy edge. When these places afterwards came into the hands of the Moabites, their ancient names were restored to them; and it is by those old names, not the new ones, that the prophets speak of them.
39:
The narrative now turns back on itself, and the tense is the question. Ellicott renders the opening as a pluperfect — now the children of Machir the son of Manasseh had gone to Gilead, and taken it — and treats the verse as the explanation, offered belatedly, of why half Manasseh appeared in the grant at all. Keil and Delitzsch agree that the imperfects are to be understood as pluperfects, and give the reason from Hebrew style rather than from convenience: the leading thought is preceded by the clauses that explain it instead of being logically subordinated to them, so that the sentence runs "the sons of Machir went to Gilead and took it… and Moses gave," where a Western writer would have put the giving first.

Calvin weighs the alternative honestly before setting it aside. It does not seem to him suitable to suppose that these victories were won after Moses had already granted the eastern country to Reuben and Gad; the reason for the exception is rather that the sons of Manasseh were not to be defrauded of lands they had separately acquired. Nor is it probable that, the country having been given to others, they afterwards made an incursion to appropriate what did not belong to them — and the order of the narrative does not require it, since it is common with the Hebrews to transpose the order of occurrences, especially when something omitted earlier is added to explain what has just been done. Yet he will not press it: if any should prefer to believe that they were attracted by the advantage that presented itself, he says, he will not pertinaciously contend the point.

Gill is careful about which Gilead is meant, since the word has done double duty all through the chapter. What Machir's sons took was the part still in Amorite hands, and not the district the two tribes had asked for; half Mount Gilead and its cities, given to Reuben and Gad, was already conquered ground, which is why the petitioners could describe it as the country the LORD smote before Israel. Keil and Delitzsch mark out the Manassite share on the map — the whole kingdom of Bashan, including the province of Bashan and the northern half of Gilead, of which the sons of Machir received Gilead itself, the modern Jebel Ajlun between the Zerka and the Mandhur — and say plainly why they received it: because they had taken it, and driven the Amorites out.

On the grant that follows, Gill and Wesley correct a natural misreading of the name. Moses gave Gilead unto Machir, but not to the man: some, Gill reports on Aben Ezra's authority, held that Machir was still alive and received it himself, which is not probable, since of all who came out of Egypt aged twenty and upward only two men were left alive. Wesley says the same in a line — not to Machir himself, who was doubtless long since dead, but to the family or posterity of Machir.
41:
The second conqueror named has a genealogy that does not run the way genealogies usually run. Gill states the anomaly at once: Jair is called the son of Manasseh by his mother's side, being otherwise of the family of Judah, for Hezron of Judah married a daughter of Machir the son of Manasseh, and had by her a son called Segub, who was Jair's father. Ellicott sets out the same descent and draws the conclusion: Jair was the great-grandson of Manasseh, and one of those Israelites who were reckoned as belonging to their maternal tribe.

Keil and Delitzsch, working from the genealogy in Chronicles, add the explanation nobody else attempts. Contrary to the ordinary rule, it was Segub — and his descendants after him — who went over into the maternal tribe, and they suggest a reason: Machir had probably portioned his daughter with a rich dowry, as though she were an heiress, which in Israelite practice was exactly the circumstance that could carry a family across a tribal line. The same commentators give the extent of Jair's conquest: he took possession of the whole province of Argob in Bashan, in the plain of Jaulan and Hauran, and gave the towns he had taken the name Havvoth Jair (Deuteronomy 3:14). Clarke thinks the name should have been translated rather than transliterated in the English text, and gives its sense — the villages, or habitations, of Jair.

Clarke then quotes Ainsworth for an observation that reaches far past the verse, and it is the sombre note the whole eastern settlement ends on. These two tribes and a half were the first in Israel to have their inheritance assigned to them in the promised land; and they were the first of all Israel to be carried captive out of their own land, because of their sins. The record Ainsworth cites is unsparing — that they transgressed against the God of their fathers and went a whoring after the gods of the peoples of the land, until God delivered them into the hands of Pul and of Tiglath-Pileser, kings of Assyria, who carried them to Halah and Habor and Hara, and to the river Gozan (1 Chronicles 5:25-26). The men naming towns after themselves on this frontier are founding the first Israelite settlement in the land of promise and, as it turned out, the first to be emptied.
42:
The chapter ends with a third conqueror and a third name fixed to the map, and about this one the record is nearly silent. Gill admits as much: who this Nobah was is not certain, though very probably he was a descendant of Manasseh. He passes on what tradition supplied — that Nobah was among those born in Egypt, and died after the death of Moses, and was buried beyond Jordan, as Machir and Jair were also said to have been, so that of that generation none were left but Caleb and Joshua. Wesley is content with the inference the context forces: though Nobah is named nowhere else, he was doubtless an eminent person of the tribe of Manasseh. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same conclusion by a different road, taking him to have belonged, like Jair, to one of the families of the Machirites, and noting that his own family is never referred to at all.

The town he took is better documented than the man. Kenath and its daughters — that is, Keil and Delitzsch explain, the smaller towns dependent upon it — are named again only where Chronicles records that Geshur and Aram afterwards took them from Israel (1 Chronicles 2:23). They identify it with the Kanatha that Josephus and Ptolemy assign to Coelesyria and Pliny to the Decapolis, and which Jerome placed in the region of Trachonitis, near Bostra; its ruins run two and a half to three miles in circumference and include magnificent remains of palaces from the times of Trajan. They decline Kurtz's identification of the place with the village of Nowa, and observe that Nobah's own name has not been preserved anywhere on the ground.

That is the quiet irony the chapter closes on, and Clarke has already supplied the frame for it: conquerors called the cities they took after their own names, and Kenath was called Nobah after the man who took it. The name did not hold. Wesley draws the larger version of the same reversal, and it answers the opening of the chapter exactly: as these tribes were placed before the other tribes, so they were displaced before them, being carried captive by the king of Assyria some years earlier than their brethren. Such a proportion, he says, does providence frequently observe in balancing prosperity and adversity — the first to be settled, and the first to be swept away.
